questions.q: In what order does this lesson recommend structuring a credible capstone write-up?
options: Limitations, qualitative examples, metrics, methodology
Methodology, metrics, qualitative examples, limitations
Metrics only — the other sections are optional
Qualitative examples first, then nothing else is needed
questions.explain: The lesson lays out methodology (task, reward code, hyperparameters), metrics (pass rate with set size), qualitative examples (a win and a miss), and limitations, in that order.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend including the exact reward function code in the methodology section, rather than just describing it in prose?
options: Code is required by convention and has no functional purpose in a write-up
So a reviewer could independently spot a reward-hacking loophole themselves, the same scrutiny the capstone's own lesson 67 applied before training
Because prose descriptions of code are not allowed in technical write-ups
Because the code is shorter than a prose description
questions.explain: Including the actual reward function lets a reader verify it isn't exploitable, mirroring the adversarial-testing mindset lesson 67 taught for the reward function itself.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a write-up that reports limitations honestly is more convincing than one that only reports the win number?
options: Because limitations are legally required in all technical writing

Because a write-up honest about where results would break (model size, budget, task narrowness) gives a reader a realistic sense of what the result does and doesn't demonstrate, rather than an inflated claim
Because reporting limitations always doubles the length of a write-up, which readers prefer
Because limitations are more important than the actual results
questions.explain: Specific limitations let a reader correctly scope what the capstone result actually shows, rather than overgeneralizing from a narrow experiment.

questions.q: This capstone trained with PPO against a verifiable reward (RLVR). Which next direction does the lesson suggest for directly comparing against this same setup on identical data?
options: Switching to Q-learning from Chapter 2
Running DPO (Chapter 7) on the same task and data
Abandoning verifiable rewards entirely in favor of human preference labels
Re-running the exact same PPO configuration with a different random seed only
questions.explain: The lesson names DPO, covered in Chapter 7 alongside PPO in the RLHF pipeline context, as the natural next comparison on identical data.

questions.q: According to this lesson's closing synthesis, why was Chapter 9's verifiable-reward concept (RLVR) necessary background for this capstone, distinct from the reward modeling covered in Chapter 6?
options: It wasn't necessary; Chapter 6's reward model is what the capstone actually used
Chapter 9 showed that feedback doesn't always need a learned model at all, which is exactly the approach this capstone implemented end to end instead of training a Bradley-Terry reward model
RLVR and reward modeling are the same technique with different names
Chapter 9 was about agentic RL, unrelated to reward signals
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts Chapter 6's learned reward model with Chapter 9's verifiable-reward approach, which this capstone used directly instead of training a reward model.
